guideTitle: Bluetooth Tracker vs GPS Tracker: 6 Picks in 2026
metaDescription: We compared four Bluetooth trackers and two true GPS trackers on network, battery, subscriptions and use case to help you pick the right type for keys or cars.
introParagraphs: Bluetooth trackers and GPS trackers get lumped together because both promise to find lost things, but they work in very different ways. A Bluetooth tag rings when you are nearby and, when it is far away, borrows other people's phones through a crowd network to report its location. A GPS tracker has its own satellite receiver and reports in real time, usually with a paid plan, which makes it the tool for vehicles and assets rather than keys.

We evaluated six products based on product specs and buyer feedback: four Bluetooth trackers (Tile, KIUP, Tracee and UGREEN FineTrack) and two true GPS trackers (LandAirSea 54 and Bouncie). Listings that call themselves GPS but actually rely on a Bluetooth crowd network were left out, because they belong on the Bluetooth side of this comparison. We compared network, battery, water resistance, platform support and subscription needs.
Use the picks, then the decision tables, to decide whether you need a tag, a card or a real-time tracker.

products.name: Life360 Tile Bluetooth Tracker, iOS and Android
specs: Rings the tag from the app
Rings your phone from the tag
products.description:
The Tile is the straightforward answer for a household with both iPhones and Android phones, because it works on both through its own app and network. You can ring a misplaced Tile or track it in the free app, and the tag can also make your phone ring even when it is silenced. A discreet SOS alert can notify loved ones, and the tags can be added to Life360 to appear on a shared family map.

The tradeoff is that Tile relies on its own network rather than the larger Apple Find My crowd, and the listing does not state the battery or range. It is a Bluetooth tag, so it will not give real-time updates when the item is far away and unmonitored. The listing covers single tags, multi-packs and an Essentials set, which are all the same family, so we count them as one pick.

In ownership, you attach a tag to keys, a bag or a bottle, pair it in the app and ring it as needed. Compared with the UGREEN, which is iOS only but lists a 2-year battery, the Tile works across phones. Against the LandAirSea 54, it will not report in real time, but it also has no subscription listed for basic finding.
products.bestFor: Mixed iPhone and Android households that want one tag type for keys, bags and a phone finder.

Sold as single tags, multi-packs and sets

Not a real-time tracker like the GPS units in this list

products.name: UGREEN FineTrack Air Tracker Tags, iOS Only, 4 Pack
products.description:
The UGREEN FineTrack Air tags pair with an iPhone or iPad in one tap through the pre-installed Find My app, which gives them access to Apple's crowd network when an item is out of range. The replaceable battery is listed at up to 2 years, which is longer than the roughly 1 year of many trackers, and the tags are Apple MFi certified with end-to-end encryption. When a tag moves out of range, the Find My app sends a lost alert with the last known location, and Lost Mode is available.

The obvious limit is platform. These are iOS only, so an Android phone cannot find or pair them, and no GPS tracking is involved, so there is no real-time position when no iPhones are nearby. The 4 pack covers keys, a wallet, a bag and a remote, but it is not a good fit for a mixed household.

In ownership, battery checks are available in the app and swapping the battery extends life. Next to the KIUP, it uses a replaceable battery rather than a sealed one, and compared with the Tile it gives up Android support in return for the Find My network. It is also a better fit for a keys-and-bags routine than for vehicle tracking.
products.bestFor: iPhone households that want a four-tag set with a long-lasting replaceable battery.
pros: Uses the Apple Find My network for far-away finding
Replaceable battery listed up to 2 years

Lost Mode and out-of-range alerts with last known location
cons: iOS only, so Android phones cannot use it

products.name: KIUP Wallet Tracker Card, Find My and Find Hub
specs: Works with Find My and Find Hub

specList.label: Networks
specList.value: Apple Find My and Google Find Hub

products.description:
The KIUP is a credit-card-thin tracker at 0.06 inches, designed to slip into a wallet or passport holder. It is listed as working with both Apple Find My and Google Find Hub, which is rare, and adds a built-in speaker rated up to 120dB, IP68 water resistance and UWB distance display within Bluetooth range. The battery is listed at 5 to 10 years, which is the longest of the group.

The cost of a sealed, thin design is that the battery is not replaceable, so the card is replaced when it dies. The listing says it is not for GPS, so it is a crowd-network tracker like the others, and a given card connects to one platform at a time. A card suits wallets more than keyrings, because it is not designed to be punched or clipped.

Setup is quick and the app shows distance and a ringing option. Compared with the Tracee, which has a replaceable 12-month battery, the KIUP trades replaceability for longevity. Against the LandAirSea 54, it is for finding a wallet in a coat pocket, not following a vehicle in real time.
products.bestFor: Wallet and passport tracking for people who want a slim card that works on iPhone or Android.
pros: Only 0.06 inches thick, so it fits a wallet
Listed as compatible with Find My and Find Hub
Built-in speaker rated up to 120dB for close-range finding
IP68 water resistance and UWB distance display
cons: Sealed battery means replacing the whole card
Connects to only one phone platform at a time
Not a GPS tracker, as the listing states

products.name: Tracee Bluetooth Locator, 2 Pack, iOS and Android
specs: Works with Find My and Google network

specList.label: Networks
specList.value: Apple Find My and Google Find My Device

products.description:
The Tracee 2 pack is built for people who want a swap-the-battery tag that works on both iPhone and Android. The listing says it connects to the Apple Find My network and the Google Find My Device network, with no monthly fee, and offers up to 12 months of use on a replaceable battery. It has an IP67 rating, a magnetic silicone case and separation alerts that warn you when the Bluetooth connection is lost.

The name says GPS, but it is a Bluetooth locator, so it relies on crowd networks rather than its own satellite receiver and will not give live position without nearby phones. A 12-month battery means yearly swaps, which is shorter than the UGREEN at 2 years and the KIUP at 5 to 10. A backup battery is included, so the first swap needs no extra purchase.

In use, you slip the tracker into the silicone case, attach it to keys or a bag and pair it to your platform. Compared with the Tile, it uses the larger crowd networks of Apple and Google. Next to the UGREEN, it works on Android as well, but it lists a shorter battery life.
products.bestFor: Mixed phone households that want a replaceable battery and separation alerts for keys and bags.
pros: Works with Apple and Google networks, no monthly fee
Replaceable battery listed up to 12 months
Separation alerts warn when you leave an item
Includes cases, keychains and a backup battery
cons: Name says GPS but it is a Bluetooth locator
12 month battery means a replacement about once a year
No live position unless a phone in the network is nearby

products.name: LandAirSea 54 GPS Tracker, Magnetic, Subscription Required
specs: Updates as fast as every 3 seconds
products.description:
The LandAirSea 54 is a true GPS tracker for vehicles, ATVs, golf carts and other assets, with updates as fast as every 3 seconds. You watch it on a web dashboard or the SilverCloud app, set geofences and alerts, and play back history for up to a year. An internal magnet and waterproof body make it easy to hide under a vehicle, and a motion-activated sleep mode preserves battery when nothing moves.

Its requirement is a subscription for each device, with plans offered monthly or annually and no contract. That makes it a poor choice for keys, where a one-time Bluetooth tag is enough, but a good one for a car, trailer or boat that you need to follow while it moves. It is larger than any Bluetooth tag here, and the listing does not give a battery life figure.

In ownership, you activate a plan, attach the unit and open the app or website. Compared with the Bouncie, which plugs into the OBD2 port and adds driving data, the LandAirSea is a stand-alone magnetic unit that you can move between assets. Against the Tile, it gives live tracking but costs ongoing fees.
products.bestFor: Following a vehicle, trailer or piece of equipment in real time with a hidden magnetic unit.
pros: Updates as fast as every 3 seconds with live alerts
Magnetic mount lets you move it between vehicles or assets
Geofences, alerts and up to 1 year of history playback
Lifetime warranty on manufacturing defects
cons: Subscription plan required for each device it tracks
Overkill for keys and wallets, where a tag is enough
No battery life figure given in the product listing

products.name: Bouncie GPS Tracker for Vehicles, OBD2

specList.label: Monitoring
specList.value: Speed, braking, idle time, engine data

products.description:
The Bouncie is an OBD2 plug-in tracker for cars, powered by the vehicle so there is no battery to charge. It reports real-time location, unlimited trip history, speed, hard braking, acceleration and idle time, and it monitors engine diagnostics to flag maintenance issues. Geofencing and accident detection are included, which makes it popular with parents of new drivers and small fleets.

The tradeoffs are plain. It only works in a vehicle with an OBD2 port, which the listing says covers most 1996 and newer models, and it needs a monthly subscription. Because it is plugged in, it is easier for a driver to find than the hidden LandAirSea magnet. It is also useless for tracking a wallet or luggage.

Installation takes seconds, since you push it into the port and set it up in the app. Compared with the LandAirSea 54, it gives driving behavior and engine data rather than moving between assets. Against any of the four Bluetooth trackers, it answers a different question: where is my car now, and how is it being driven.
products.bestFor: Families and small fleets who want live location plus driving and engine data from a plug-in unit.
pros: Plugs into the OBD2 port, so no battery to charge
Real-time location with unlimited trip history
Tracks speed, hard braking and engine health
Geofencing and accident detection included
cons: Monthly subscription required for the tracking service
Only works in vehicles with an OBD2 port
Easy for a driver to spot and unplug from the port

buyingCriteria.explanation: Bluetooth trackers ring when you are near and report through a crowd network of other phones when far, while GPS trackers have their own receiver and report on their own. The Tile, UGREEN, KIUP and Tracee are Bluetooth tags, while the LandAirSea 54 updates as fast as every 3 seconds and the Bouncie reports in real time. If you need a position that updates while a car is moving, choose GPS. For keys and wallets, a tag is enough.

Apple Find My trackers work with iPhone only, while Google Find Hub trackers serve Android, and some trackers certify for only one network. The UGREEN is iOS only, the Tile works on both through its own app, and the Tracee and KIUP list both Find My and Google support. A given tag typically connects to one platform at a time. Check your household's phones before buying.

Bluetooth tags rely on crowd networks and list no monthly fee, such as the Tracee and UGREEN. GPS trackers need a plan, with the LandAirSea 54 requiring a subscription for each device and the Bouncie requiring a monthly plan. Over several years, the plan cost usually exceeds the hardware cost. Decide whether live tracking justifies it.

Replaceable coin cells last about a year and let the tag keep going, while sealed batteries last longer but mean replacing the device. The Tracee lists 12 months replaceable, the UGREEN up to 2 years replaceable, and the KIUP 5 to 10 years sealed. The Bouncie draws power from the OBD2 port. For fewest chores, pick the longest listed life.

Bluetooth range is limited to roughly 100 to 400 ft depending on model and walls, and far finding depends on nearby phones. In a city, crowd networks work well, but on a remote road they may give no update. That is the real gap versus GPS. The KIUP adds UWB distance display within range, and the UGREEN and Tile use their networks when far.

A keyring tag, a wallet card and a vehicle unit each need different durability. The KIUP is IP68 at 0.06 inches thick, the Tracee is IP67 with a magnetic silicone case, and the LandAirSea 54 is waterproof with an internal magnet. IP67 handles splashes and brief immersion. Match the shape to where the tracker will live.

howWeEvaluated.title: Tracking method and network
howWeEvaluated.description: We first sorted each product by how it locates itself. The Tile, UGREEN, KIUP and Tracee use Bluetooth with crowd networks, while the LandAirSea 54 and Bouncie are real-time GPS trackers. Products labeled GPS that actually used a Bluetooth network were treated as Bluetooth.

howWeEvaluated.title: Platform compatibility
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked which phones each product supports. The UGREEN is iOS only, the Tile works on iOS and Android, and the Tracee and KIUP list both Apple and Google networks. Broader compatibility scored higher for mixed households.

howWeEvaluated.title: Battery and upkeep
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared battery type and listed life: the KIUP at 5 to 10 years sealed, the UGREEN at up to 2 years replaceable and the Tracee at 12 months replaceable. The Bouncie takes power from the vehicle. Fewer chores earned credit.

howWeEvaluated.title: Durability and form factor
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at water resistance and shape, including the KIUP's IP68 and 0.06 inch thickness, the Tracee's IP67 and silicone case, and the LandAirSea 54's waterproof magnetic body. Fit for the intended item counted.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ongoing cost and fit
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered whether a subscription is required and whether the product suits its job. The LandAirSea 54 and Bouncie need plans, while the four Bluetooth products list none. We did not rank on price figures, only on how well each fits its use.

faq.q: What is the main difference between a Bluetooth tracker and a GPS tracker?
faq.a: A Bluetooth tracker rings when you are nearby and uses a crowd network of other phones when far, while a GPS tracker has its own receiver and reports on its own. The Tile and UGREEN are Bluetooth tags, and the LandAirSea 54 and Bouncie are GPS. Bluetooth fits keys, GPS fits vehicles.

faq.q: Do Bluetooth trackers need a subscription?
faq.a: The Bluetooth trackers here list no monthly fee. GPS trackers usually do, with the LandAirSea 54 requiring a plan for each device and the Bouncie a monthly plan. Check the plan before you buy.

faq.q: Can a Bluetooth tracker work like GPS?
faq.a: Not really. It reports location only when another phone in its network passes nearby, so a remote area may give no update. A GPS tracker reports on its own. Some listings use the word GPS for Bluetooth tags, so read the details.

faq.q: Which tracker works with both iPhone and Android?
faq.a: The Tile works on both through its own app. The Tracee and KIUP list both Apple and Google networks, though a tag generally connects to one platform at a time. The UGREEN is iOS only, so check your phones first.

faq.q: How long do the batteries last?
faq.a: The Tracee lists up to 12 months on a replaceable battery, the UGREEN up to 2 years, and the KIUP 5 to 10 years sealed. The Bouncie draws power from the OBD2 port. Replaceable cells let you keep the tag, sealed ones mean replacing it.

faq.q: Can a tracker stop someone from stealing my car?
faq.a: No. Trackers locate items, they do not prevent theft. A GPS unit like the LandAirSea 54 can show where a vehicle is moving, which helps recovery, but you should contact police rather than confront anyone.

faq.q: Will a tracker warn me if someone slips one into my bag?
faq.a: Certified trackers on phone networks include unwanted tracking alerts that tell you when an unknown tag travels with you. These protect privacy, and they are one reason to choose certified trackers over unbranded ones.
